<div class="page-hero-inner">
<div class="eyebrow">Teaching</div>
<h1>Economics starts with questions students actually want to answer.</h1>
<p>My teaching philosophy is built around motivation: students learn more deeply when formal tools are connected to real economic questions from the start.</p>
</div>
</header>
<section class="content-band">
<p class="section-kicker">Teaching Philosophy</p>
<h2 class="section-title">Motivation is not a reward after the model. It is the entry point.</h2>
<div class="grid-two">
<div>
<p class="section-lede">I design courses backward from economic questions that students can recognize as meaningful. Once those questions are on the table, the underlying concepts and formal tools have a purpose: they help students discipline intuition, clarify assumptions, and make better arguments.</p>
<p class="section-lede">This structure helps students see economics as a way of reasoning through real problems rather than a sequence of isolated techniques. The goal is not only technical competence, but judgment about when a concept applies and what its limits are.</p>
<div class="action-row" style="margin-top: 1.5rem;">
<a class="inline-link" href="teaching_statement.pdf">Read teaching statement</a>
<a class="inline-link" href="../../index.html">Back to home</a>
</div>
</div>
<aside class="note-panel">
<h3>Teaching statement</h3>
<p>The full statement explains how I use backward design, motivating questions, and carefully sequenced formal tools to build student engagement in economics.</p>
<div class="paper-links">

</div>
</aside>
</div>
</section>
<section class="content-band tint">
<p class="section-kicker">Course Design</p>
<h2 class="section-title">A simple sequence that keeps the work grounded.</h2>
<div class="grid-three">
<article class="teaching-card">
<h3>Start With The Question</h3>
<p>Identify economic questions that connect with students' backgrounds, goals, and the institutional context of the course.</p>
</article>
<article class="teaching-card">
<h3>Build The Concept</h3>
<p>Show how the question becomes an instance of a core economic idea, and why one framework is useful while another may not be.</p>
</article>
<article class="teaching-card">
<h3>Introduce The Tool</h3>
<p>Bring in math and models when they become necessary for sharpening intuition, analyzing tradeoffs, and interpreting results.</p>
</article>
</div>
</section>
<section class="quote-band">
<blockquote>
    Students should leave with judgment about how and when to apply economic reasoning.
<cite>Teaching philosophy</cite>
</blockquote>
</section>
<section class="content-band">
<p class="section-kicker">Classroom Commitments</p>
<h2 class="section-title">What students should feel in the room.</h2>
<div class="timeline">
<div class="timeline-item">
<div class="time">Relevance</div>
<div>
<h3>The material should have a visible reason to exist.</h3>
<p>Early course time is used to connect economic concepts to questions students can see in policy, markets, institutions, and everyday decision-making.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="timeline-item">
<div class="time">Connection</div>
<div>
<h3>Concepts should accumulate instead of fragmenting.</h3>
<p>New topics are introduced by showing what previous concepts explain well, where they fail, and why the next framework is needed.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="timeline-item">
<div class="time">Interpretation</div>
<div>
<h3>Formal results should be read as economic arguments.</h3>
<p>Models are treated as disciplined representations of reasoning, with emphasis on assumptions, scope, and interpretation rather than calculation alone.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
